text.p: (Compiled for Reuters by Media Monitors)
THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

The government's plan to deregulate Australia's A$20 billion telecommunications industry is in jeopardy, following outcry against proposed new rules by global communications companies, including British Telecom. Their main fear is that the changes will allow Telstra and Optus to take advantage of a liberal regulatory environment to restrict competition. Page 1.

Although Australian Treasurer Peter Costello probably won't be invited back to the U.S. Federal Reserve again following his indiscretions earlier this week, it appears Reserve chief Dr Alan Greenspan believes there will be no rise in the rate of inflation in the U.S. for the time being. Page 1.

Queensland developer Keith Williams' Port Hinchinbrook development has been stalled after an environment group won an injunction yesterday in the Federal Court preventing work to continue on the controversial project. The injunction temporarily stops the developer from lopping mangrove trees at the Hinchinbrook site. Page 3.

Federal public service senior executive Mike Jones has predicted the Commonwealth public service could be reduced from its present workforce of 130,000 to 50,000 by the year 2000. Jones, speaking at a Foreign Affairs Department South and South East Asia division meeting, stressed he was not speaking on behalf of the government. Industrial Relations Minister Peter Reith denied the prediction claiming the government's approach was not "numbers driven." Page 3.
THE AUSTRALIAN

Documents due to be released today by the United States Government reveal intercepted cables to Moscow from KGB agents in Canberra provide the first documentary evidence of a Soviet spy ring which infiltrated the Australian Government to steal secret Allied documents in the 1940s. Page 1.

The Tasmanian Government yesterday moved to freeze the assets of alleged Port Arthur gunman Martin Bryant as a prelude to selling them and distributing the proceeds to victims families if he is convicted. The unique legislation places Bryant's A$1 million assets in control of the courts once the legislation is proclaimed. Tasmanian Attorney-General Ray Groom said the bill was not Bryant-specific, as it could be applied to anyone charged with a serious offence. Page 1.

According to the latest Australian Newspoll, 71 percent of voters believe Australian immigration levels are too high, with only two percent saying the intake was "too low". This has come as welcome news for the federal government which decided to cut immigration levels for this financial year by 11 percent to 74,000. Page 1.

The governments of Australia's two biggest states, Victoria and New South Wales, have threatened to hold their own inquiry into the taxation system if the federal government continues to ignore calls for reform. The suggestion was raised yesterday by Vicorian Premier Jeff Kennett and welcomed immediately by New South Wales Treasurer Michael Egan on behalf of the country's only current Labor government. Page 1.
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

The New South Wales Supreme Court was told yesterday the 22-year-old man accused of killing British tourist Brian Hagland at Bondi Beach last month has an "attraction for brutal violence". The comments were made by Crown Prosecutor Chris Maxwell, QC, moving to oppose a bail application by the defendant Aaron Lee Martin. Page 1.

More than 5,000 mourners packed Western Australia's Gracetown cliffs carpark yesterday to honour the group of parents, teachers and children crushed by tonnes of rock when a cliff gave-way during an interschool surf contest last Friday. Page 1.

South Coast Labor Party Branch Tuross Head, located just south of Moruya, has pledged its qualified support for the views of maverick Independent MP Pauline Hanson just as Prime Minister John Howard is under new pressure to reject Hanson's latest statements on immigration in order to protect trade with Asia. Page 1.

Eighty community and church groups, led by the Australian Council of Social Service (ACOSS), made a plea to the minor parties holding balance of power in the Senate to support amendments that would defeat major parts of the federal government's proposed workplace relations legislation. The groups warned that the proposals would turn Australia into a low-wage country and increase poverty levels. Page 2.
THE AGE

The federal government's health-insurance strategy, promising private health insurance cuts, came under questioning again yesterday, as another insurance fund, National Mutual, announced increases in average premiums of 5.1 percent to 10.3 percent for South Australia, Western Australia and the Northern Territory. Health Minister Michael Wooldridge defended the rises labelling them as "nothing unusual". Page A1.

Federal Treasurer Peter Costello is under intense pressure as he continues to deny he revealed sensitive details of a conversation with U.S. Federal Reserve head Dr Alan Greenspan. Despite reverberations in financial markets around the world, Costello insists he did not give out "special information". Page A1.

The Australian Securities Commission is investigating possible breeches of the Corporations Law, meeting with surveillance analysts from the Australian Stock Exchange yesterday, after heavy trading in TNT share options just prior to a A$2 billion takeover bid by the Dutch group KPN. Page A1.

The Australian Council of Social Services yesterday warned that over a quarter of workers will face poverty if the federal government's workplace reforms are passed by the Senate in their current form. A coalition of over 80 social welfare groups sent a joint statement to members of the Senate, urging them to amend the Workplace Relations Bill. Page A3.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 373-1800
